item.title: Testing on other hosts
item.description:
For contributors. The everyday tests, CLI tests and end-to-end tests are in Contributing, and how to raise a package’s coverage baseline is in Coverage; this page is about running them on a host other than your Mac.

What’s platform-specific

The same code and tests run on macOS and Linux; what differs is behind build tags in internal/platform and the backend’s own checks:

macOS Linux
VMs Lima on Apple’s Virtualization framework (vz) Lima on QEMU with KVM
Mounts virtiofs 9p, one mount per share per guest
Project VM disks APFS copy-on-write clones of the image’s qcow2 overlays of the image’s
Confined tiers the VM’s Lima process under a macOS sandbox QEMU’s restrict=on and a guestfwd to the proxy
.git protection locked with chflags read-only in QEMU’s namespace, or, where the kernel refuses it, watched, and devvm says so (details)
Set-id files dropped by virtiofs reach the host: new VMs check for them
Tokens the Keychain files only you can read, in ~/.local/share/devvm/secrets/
The CA kept out of Time Machine no backup to keep it out of

The end-to-end tests check each side where they run: on Linux, the .git protection checks look at QEMU’s namespace and what root in the VM can do, or, on a host whose kernel refuses the namespace, that it’s off and devvm says so, and the Keychain check is left out. The CLI tests run as on a Linux host that can’t pin (DEVVM_PINS), whatever the host’s kernel allows, and the unit tests that pin for real (TestRunPinned, TestProbePin) run only on a Linux host that allows it.

On macOS, the end-to-end tests also need OpenSSL as openssl, because its CA checks serve HTTPS with openssl s_server, and the LibreSSL that macOS ships as /usr/bin/openssl cuts the VM’s OpenSSL client off mid-request. Install it with brew install openssl@3, then put $(brew --prefix openssl@3)/bin first on your PATH, because Homebrew doesn’t link it into its own bin. On Linux, openssl is OpenSSL, and Ubuntu’s images have it installed, as ca-certificates needs it.

Before it builds anything, the runner checks every command of this machine’s that the chosen sections use. It always checks limactl and pkill, and each section lists the others it needs in tests/e2e/sections_test.go, such as git, openssl, which must be OpenSSL and not LibreSSL, OpenSSH’s ssh, ssh-agent, ssh-add and ssh-keygen, tar, ps, lsof on macOS or ss on Linux, and python3. When any of them is missing, e2e lists each one with the command that installs it, through Homebrew on macOS or apt-get or dnf on Linux, and stops. It needs Go too, or mise, which installs the repo’s pinned Go.

Linux hosts

Test in a Lima VM with nested virtualization, which needs an M3 or newer and macOS 15 or newer. Give it a Lima home of its own, so its VMs stay apart from yours:

  1. Make it from Lima’s Ubuntu template, with nested virtualization, room for nested VMs, its user at uid 1000, and only the repo mounted, read-only:

    REPO=$(pwd) && cd /tmp
export LIMA_HOME=~/.lt-linux-go
limactl create --name=linuxhost --tty=false --vm-type=vz --cpus=8 --memory=16 --disk=150 \
 --containerd=none --set '.nestedVirtualization=true | .user.uid=1000' --mount "$REPO" template:ubuntu-24.04
limactl edit --tty=false --set '.mounts=[{"location":"'"$REPO"'","writable":false}]' linuxhost
limactl start --tty=false linuxhost

    Run it from the main checkout of the repo, which the VM mounts at the same path, and not from a git worktree. A worktree’s .git is a file that points into the main checkout’s .git folder, outside the mount, so git in the VM can’t read it, and the VM’s only mount goes when the worktree does. --mount alone keeps the template’s home mount, hence the edit. Lima gives the VM’s user your Mac’s uid unless user.uid sets another, and a Mac’s first user has uid 501. Most Linux hosts’ first user has uid 1000, and so does the user that some container images ship, such as the ubuntu user of Ubuntu’s images. With the VM’s user at uid 1000, the end-to-end tests’ from section meets that clash, as devvm does on most Linux hosts.

  2. Inside it, install the packages, then Lima and mise from their release tarballs, each checked against its release’s checksums (SHA256SUMS, SHASUMS256.txt) with sha256sum -c, and add yourself to the kvm group:

    sudo apt-get install -y qemu-system-arm qemu-utils qemu-efi-aarch64 virtiofsd build-essential git curl jq rsync
sudo usermod -aG kvm "$USER"

    Then restart the VM, so a fresh login has the group.

  3. Copy the repo into the VM’s home, so the read-only mount stays untouched, install the pinned tools and run the gate, then the end-to-end tests:

    rsync -a --delete /path/to/your/checkout/ ~/devvm/ && cd ~/devvm
mise trust && mise install
mise run fmt && mise run lint && mise run test
mise run e2e -- --from

    The copy keeps the checkout’s .git folder, which the gate needs, because mise run lint finds the shell scripts it checks with git ls-files, and the docs’ build reads each page’s git information (enableGitInfo). A copy without .git, such as one that git archive makes, fails the lint. To test a branch that a worktree has checked out, commit it, and clone that branch from the main checkout instead of copying the checkout, because a worktree’s branches are the main checkout’s too:

    rm -rf ~/devvm && git clone --branch BRANCH /path/to/your/checkout ~/devvm && cd ~/devvm

    A clone has only what’s committed, so commit a change before you test it this way.

The first --from run builds every image and takes about half an hour on an M3 Max. Later ones reuse them, because every section but tools uses the pinned shared tools’ versions and --from images, and those images stay valid until scripts/bump.sh e2e-tools or scripts/bump.sh e2e-from moves a pin (end-to-end tests). Stop the VM when done (limactl stop linuxhost); it keeps its images for the next run.

Gotchas of this setup:

  • The Linux host’s home and its VMs’ homes are both /home/<user>.guest, so a file under $HOME in a VM isn’t proof of a mount: the end-to-end tests check the VM’s mounts list instead.
  • A VM booting while another one works boots degraded and its downloads time out: the end-to-end tests stop a VM it’s done with before starting the next.
  • minisign, for signing releases, has no linux/arm64 build, so mise skips it there.

x86_64 hosts

These need real x86_64 hardware, or an x86_64 VM on such hardware with nested virtualization. An emulated x86_64 VM on a Mac (--arch=x86_64, QEMU TCG; Lima needs its lima-additional-guestagents) runs the unit tests, but VMs nested in it crash in their firmware.

A bare-metal x86_64 Linux host, such as Fedora 43 with SELinux enforcing, runs the gate and mise run e2e -- --from as the Linux host above does, from a clone of the repo, and it can run --slots 3 (slots for each host). Those runs check the x86_64 side of what devvm builds: the _amd64 pins of base, every layer and feature, the shared tools’ linux-x64 lock entries and their checksums, --from’s conversion, whose VM reads its scripts over 9p, and the confined tiers through devvm _qemu and qemu-system-x86_64.

The tests don’t cover the release itself, so check it by hand on that host. Build the archives with scripts/release.sh --head, with DEVVM_MINISIGN_KEY and DEVVM_MINISIGN_PUB naming a test key so the signature is checked too, and install devvm-<version>-linux-amd64.tar.gz from them in a throwaway HOME, as maintaining shows, with main --yes in place of main --no-deps. With only the system’s folders on PATH, the script finds no Lima, so it installs Lima’s latest release into that HOME’s ~/.local. When the host already has QEMU and access to /dev/kvm, nothing it runs needs sudo. Then run the installed devvm --version and devvm doctor, and check with file that the binary is statically linked.

devvm hasn’t been tested on an Intel Mac. Its release has a darwin-amd64 archive, and that binary runs under Rosetta on Apple silicon, but nobody has run the tests or a VM on Intel hardware.

GitHub’s Linux runners are x86_64 with KVM, and the E2E workflow (.github/workflows/e2e.yml) runs mise run e2e -- --only project on one as a trial. Start it from the repo’s Actions tab, with Run workflow on the E2E workflow, because it has no other trigger yet. It installs QEMU, gives the runner’s user /dev/kvm as Lima’s own CI does, installs Lima at a pinned version checked against its checksum, and runs the section up to three times. It caches Ubuntu’s cloud image under the release that the end-to-end tests pin, and the built images under a hash of assets/, tests/e2e-mise.lock, that release and Lima’s version, because devvm’s image keys are only known once it builds. When the run fails, it uploads the e2e logs, devvm’s run logs and each Lima instance’s serial logs as the e2e-logs artifact.

Slots for each host

mise run e2e -- --slots N runs the end-to-end sections in N sandboxes at once (slots), and each slot runs its own VMs, up to three at a time in the link section. How many slots a host can run depends on its cores and memory:

Host Slots
A bare-metal Linux host with 32 cores and 124 GB of memory 3 or 4
A Mac 2
A Linux host nested in a VM, such as the Linux host above 1, the default: a VM booting while another one works boots degraded there

A Mac clones the images it gives each slot, because /tmp and your home folder are on the same APFS volume. A Linux host reflinks the Lima instances in your home folder when its file system can, as XFS made with reflink=1 and Btrfs can, but a /tmp on tmpfs can’t reflink, so there each slot other than slot 0 builds its own tool images. Every slot keeps its images between runs, so only its first run builds them.

End-to-end tests in Go

The end-to-end tests are in Go, in tests/e2e, a file for each section. That package builds only with the e2e build tag, and its TestE2E is the run.

Running the runner

mise run e2e runs TestE2E from tests/e2e, with the run’s flags after --. You can also run go test yourself from that folder:

mise run e2e -- --only gc
cd tests/e2e && CGO_ENABLED=0 go test -tags e2e -count=1 -timeout 0 -run '^TestE2E$' -args --only gc

Run go test from tests/e2e without naming a package, because only then does go test show the run’s lines as they come, and in a package list it holds them until the package ends. TestE2E refuses any -timeout but 0, because go test’s default of 10 minutes would end a long section in the middle of a check, and -count=1 keeps go test from showing a cached result. The run’s flags, which Contributing lists, come after -args. --reuse keeps the VMs that a section makes with Reuse for the next run, which takes each one as it finds it when it’s still running, so iterating on one check doesn’t launch its VM again.

The runner uses a sandbox for each slot, with its own fixed ports, it refuses your real Lima home, and it builds devvm from the checkout into src-go in the sandbox’s state folder, as a test build with its files embedded. It writes a config.toml that chooses base’s features, so nothing asks, and puts the pinned tool lock in place, after checking the lock’s first line. Base starts from the dated Ubuntu release in e2eUbuntuRelease (tests/e2e/sandbox_test.go), which scripts/bump.sh e2e-ubuntu moves. The runner takes the slot’s lock, a symlink to its pid, and it deletes only the VMs, files and project folders that it made. Before anything else, it names each host command that the chosen sections need and this machine lacks, with what installs it. Its lines are each section’s == name heading, then PASS, FAIL, SKIP or RETRY with [n/N], the check’s title, its time, the run’s time and the time left. A heartbeat every minute shows the newest line of the check’s output or devvm’s run log, and the run ends with a summary line. It keeps each section’s times in slot 0’s timings folder, under its tier, and beside them a checksum of tests/e2e’s Go files, so a section’s check count is compared only with a run of the same Go files. With --slots, it plans, seeds and runs the slots, each slot a run of the same test binary, and it adds up their results. On macOS it seeds each slot with APFS clones (clonefile), and on Linux with reflinks. With --newest-base, its last lines name the release Ubuntu lists as its newest and the one devvm pinned, and a failure is named as upstream drift.

Each check’s time limit is three times its longest time in its section’s last complete run, and the steps between two checks get an hour. Each command a check runs is in a process group of its own, and when the check’s time runs out, the group gets TERM, then KILL 30 seconds later. The check then fails with the heartbeat’s last line, and the run goes on to the next check. The runner’s own tests, the TestHarness tests, need no VM, and mise run test runs them with the e2e tag.

Writing a check

A section is a function that takes the running section, *S, and calls s.Check once for each check:

s.Check("gc deletes a tool image no VM uses, with its record", func() error {
 if Exists(old) || Exists(old+".json") {
 return errors.New("the old tool image or its record is still there")
 }
 return nil
})

The check passes when its function returns nil. Its title is its key in the timings, so a changed title starts its times again: give a new check a title that says what it proves. When a check fails, the runner prints its error, each line led by failed:, and then the last 5 lines that its commands printed, or as many as Tail(n) asks for. A check that the run has nothing for is s.Skip(title, why), which counts it, so that runs compare their counts.

The commands a check runs go through the section, so that they run in the sandbox’s environment and within the check’s time limit, and their output goes into the check’s log:

Helper What it runs or reads
s.Devvm(dir, args…), s.DevvmNames(dir, args…) the run’s devvm in dir, with no input; DevvmNames in names mode (DEVVM_MESSAGES=names)
s.Msg(name, "k=v"…) a message’s text, from devvm _msg, so a check never repeats its wording
s.Limactl(args…), s.InVM(vm, script), s.Status(vm) limactl in the sandbox’s Lima home, a script in the VM’s login shell with no input, and a VM’s status
s.Run(Cmd{…}) any command, with its own folder, input or variables
s.NewProject(name), s.Launch(dir, input, args…), s.Reuse(name, input, args…) a new project folder, deleted at the end, and devvm launched in a folder, its VM recorded for the cleanup
s.Paths.State(vm), s.Paths.VMOf(dir), s.Paths.VMDir(vm) a VM’s vm.json, flattened as the CLI tests’ vm_state does, the VM a folder has, and its folder
s.Paths.KeysOf(image), s.Paths.Record(key, field), s.Own(image) an image’s keys and records, and its images made the run’s to delete
s.Layer(name, script), s.Paths a layer of the run’s (e2e*), deleted at the end, and the sandbox’s folders
s.Golden(name, args…) with --golden, a golden fixture captured from what args printed
s.GoE2E(test, pkg, "VAR=value"…) a Go test in internal/pkg that needs a real VM, such as TestE2EExecQuoting, with its variables in its environment and never in a process’s arguments
s.Until(timeout, fn), Settle a wait for what the check looks for, trying each second, and the one fixed wait, before looking for something that must not have happened
s.Port(p), s.Defer(fn) one of slot 0’s fixed ports as this slot has it, and a cleanup of the section’s own

Three options change how a check runs. Flaky(reason) marks a check that’s known to flake: when it fails, the runner shows its output and runs it once more, and only a second failure fails it. Its result says retried once, and its timings line and the summary say so too, and every other check fails on its first failure. Builds() marks a check whose own command can build base or a --from base, so it gets at least an hour. Needs(backend.FeatureLink) names the backend features that a check proves: on a backend that has one of them neither natively nor emulated and reviewed, as devvm doctor --json shows its features, the check is skipped and counted, so a check is written once for every backend that has its features. A section whose every check proves a feature takes it once with s.Needing(...), as link takes FeatureLink, nix FeatureNixLayer and --from FeatureFrom, and a section’s own checks of the docker or nix layer and of ports name theirs with Needs.

Adding a section

Each section is a file of its own in tests/e2e, such as gc_test.go, so sections can change at the same time without touching each other’s files. A new check goes in its section’s function, where its setup steps run, because a check’s time counts from the end of the one before it. To add a section:

  1. Write <section>Section(s *S) in tests/e2e/<section>_test.go.
  2. Add it to sections (tests/e2e/sections_test.go), in the order the run runs it, with a guess of its time for --slots to place it before it has run, and the host commands it needs beyond limactl and pkill, each with what installs it.
  3. Run it with mise run e2e -- --only <section> on a Mac and on a Linux host, and check that each check passes.

A helper that more than one section needs goes in the harness’s files, beside those above, so that every section shares one copy, and a fixture that two sections share, such as an image, stays in the sandbox’s cache. These are the ones the sections share so far, each with what it does in a shell’s terms:

Helper What it does In a shell
s.Start(Cmd{…}), Proc runs a command in the background, past the check that starts it, in a process group of its own, until Stop or the run’s end, with its output in Out and never in the check’s log cmd &
StartCorp(s), Corp starts a company proxy, a devvm _proxy on 127.0.0.1 at slot 0’s port 18766 as the slot has it, with a password of its own, allowing any host, and waits for it to listen; Env gives a command HTTPS_PROXY and HTTP_PROXY with its password, Saw looks for one of its events, and Addr is its address without the password corp_start, corp_stop
WriteProxyConfig(s, file, proxy.Config{…}) writes a config for devvm _proxy -config, mode 600, with the proxy’s own Config type proxy_config
NewCA(s), CA makes the run’s throwaway CA once, with a server certificate for host.lima.internal, localhost and 127.0.0.1; Trust and Untrust put it in devvm’s CA folder and take the folder away, Serve(port) serves HTTPS with it on every address until StopServing, Sign makes another server certificate, and GoneFrom(s, vm) checks that a VM keeps none of devvm’s CA files e2e_ca, ca_serve, ca_stop, ca_gone
NoLeak(secrets, paths…) fails when a regular file under the paths holds one of the secrets, or can’t be read, reading only where each file has data, as SEEK_DATA and SEEK_HOLE find it, so a VM’s sparse disk takes seconds, and naming the file but never the secret; every check that a secret is in no file on this machine uses it no_leak
GuestHasNone(s, vm, secrets, dirs…) fails when a file under the folders in the VM holds one of the secrets, searched as root, the secrets on grep’s input sudo grep -rqsFf /dev/stdin
WatchProcs(s), ProcWatch, ProcsHave(s, secret) samples every host process’s command line every 0.1 s until Stop, into a file of the sandbox’s, and Saw looks for a secret in the samples, while ProcsHave looks in one sample taken now; a check that reads either is ProcsFlaky(), as a listing can catch a short-lived process mid-start ps_watch, ps_unwatch
s.Paths.ToolVersion(tool) the tool’s version in the shared tools’ lock lockv
s.Paths.RunLogs(), s.Paths.RunLogHas(line) devvm’s run logs by name, the one reader of that folder, and whether one of them has the line, whole: what a build’s script printed logs/runs/*.log, grep -qx
MountLine(s, vm), MountsOf(s, vm) the host folders a VM’s Lima config mounts, each with a space after it, or one a line limactl list --format '{{range .Config.Mounts}}…'
HasLine, CaptureLine, ExitStatus whether text has a line, whole; the first group of the first line a regular expression matches; the exit status a command’s error says grep -qx, sed -n 's/…/\1/p', $?
launchWith(s, dir, env, args…), devvmCmd(s, dir, input, env, args…) Launch and devvm with variables of their own in devvm’s environment, such as a fake token, a HOME of the section’s or NoDocker’s PATH, never in its arguments HOME=… "$D"
vmHas(s, vm, login, script, secrets…), vmGrep(s, vm, script, re) whether what a script prints in the VM holds one of the secrets, or matches re, looked for in the VM with the secrets on its shell’s input, so neither they nor what the script printed reach the check’s log in_vm … | grep -qF
limaListens(s, proto, port), loopbackOnly(s, port) whether Lima’s own processes listen on a port of this machine, and whether what listens on one listens on loopback alone, with lsof on macOS and ss on Linux lima_listens, loopback_only
DevvmIn(s, dir, input, env, args…), OwnVM(s, vm) runs devvmCmd’s command, and makes a VM that a step launched the run’s, so that the cleanup deletes it (cd DIR && VAR=… "$D" …)
SaidLine(out, msg), FirstLine, LastLine, tailLines(text, n), Trim whether one of output’s lines is one of a message’s, a message’s first or last line, text’s last lines, and output without its trailing newlines grep -qxF "$(m …)", head -1, tail -n, $(…)
Listed(s, vm), Locked(s, file), Procs(s), Forwarders(s, vm) whether limactl lists a VM, whether a file has macOS’s user immutable flag, every host process’s command line, which stays out of the check’s log as WatchProcs’s samples do, and a VM’s port forwarders here limactl list -q, ls -lOd, ps -axww, pgrep -f '[_]ports -vm VM '
Reaches(s, addr), ReachesWithin, Answer(s, addr), Local(port), Local6(port) whether something takes a TCP connection on an address, at once or within a time, and what a connection reads before it closes, within 2 seconds nc -z, nc -w 2
HostProgram(s, addr, answer) a program on this machine that holds a port, every IPv4 address with :port, and answers each connection with host-program or accepts none perl -MIO::Socket::INET
LimaServe(s, vm, ports…), VMSay(s, vm, addr, port, word), LimaBoot(s, vm) starts servers in a VM, on every address or on one address with a word of their own, and reads the VM’s boot’s ID lima_serve, vm_say, lima_boot
PortsLive(s, dir, vm, port, serve, boot), HostPortKept(s, dir, vm, port, control, serve) checks that devvm ports add and rm apply to a running VM at once without a restart, and that a listed port a program here holds stays its own until it’s freed ports_live, host_port_kept
TTYRun(s, dir, input, args…) runs a command on a terminal of its own, script on macOS and Python’s pty on Linux, and types the input once a [y/N] or [Y/n] question shows tty_run
WatchSees(s, vm, dir, by, nested), WatchMisses(s, vm, dir) runs a file watcher in the VM and checks which changes, made in the VM or on this machine, it sees watch_sees, watch_misses
SSHAgent(s, sock), KeyComments(out), RfwdLinks(s, host, sock, ssh…) starts a throwaway ssh-agent, reads the keys’ comments from ssh-add -l, and checks that a VM’s sshd binds remote forwards only on links’ addresses ssh-agent -a, awk '{ print $3 }', rfwd_links
ExecQuoting(s, vm), ServeDesktop(s, dir, args…), Desktop runs TestE2EExecQuoting on a VM, and runs devvm desktop --no-open in the background until it says where the desktop is, which View checks with TestE2EDesktop and End ends with Ctrl+C go_e2e, desktop_serve, desktop_view, desktop_end
Note(s, format, …) adds a line of the check’s own to its log, which a failure shows among its last lines a check’s echo
SetState(s.Paths, vm, key, json) sets a dotted key of a VM’s vm.json to a JSON value by hand, as nothing devvm runs would, keeping the rest vm_set
NoDocker(s), DockerCalls(s) a PATH with a docker first on it that’s installed but not running, which logs what devvm asked it to the file DockerCalls names nd
NewestLog(s.Paths) devvm’s newest run log, the last devvm’s newest_log

A secret that a check looks for is never in a process’s arguments, where other users can see it. The company proxy’s password is in its config file and in the environment of the commands that Env is given to, and each helper above takes a secret as a Go value, so it reaches grep on its input and is never on a command line.

Test builds

The tests run a test build of devvm, which is one made with -ldflags "-X github.com/devvmhq/devvm/internal/testbuild.testBuild=yes", as the end-to-end tests and the CLI tests make theirs. Only a test build reads the environment variables that stand in for what devvm would find on this machine. Releases (GoReleaser, the Homebrew formula) don’t set the flag, so a release ignores every one of these variables, whatever its environment says. devvm reads them in one place, readOverrides in internal/cli/overrides.go, into an Overrides struct, and passes each one to the package that uses it:

Variable Stands in for
DEVVM_HOST_MISE devvm’s pinned and checked mise on the host
DEVVM_KVM Linux’s /dev/kvm
DEVVM_UBUNTU_URL https://cloud-images.ubuntu.com/releases/resolute, where devvm finds Ubuntu’s dated releases
DEVVM_UBUNTU_RELEASE the newest dated release, which devvm pins base to: the end-to-end tests pin their own, e2eUbuntuRelease, so its images stay cached between runs, and devvm checks it as it does the newest
DEVVM_UNREVIEWED the refusal of unreviewed emulations (unreviewed emulations)
DEVVM_TEST_CPUS, DEVVM_TEST_MEMORY_GIB, DEVVM_TEST_FREE_GIB, DEVVM_TEST_LIST_TIMEOUT this machine’s size and how long devvm waits for a backend’s listings (a host of any size)
DEVVM_PIPED_ANSWERS a terminal to answer questions in: with 1, each question reads its answer as a line of input that isn’t a terminal, without its prompt, where devvm would refuse it
DEVVM_HISTORY_MAX the 2 GiB that an export of agents’ history holds at most, in bytes, so a script whose VM writes an export without end reaches the cap at once

The settings that the environment table lists, such as DEVVM_LIMA_HOME, DEVVM_SECRET_SERVICE and DEVVM_NO_TOOL_CHECK, are yours to set, so every build reads them.

Tests on real Lima

Most Go tests run the limactl stub, which can’t tell whether real Lima accepts what devvm gives it. The tests in internal/backend/lima/real_test.go run the real limactl instead, on dummy instances, as Lima’s own tests do. A dummy instance’s image is a small local file, so it can’t boot, but limactl still creates, clones, edits, lists and deletes it. The tests run in a sandbox of their own, with a Lima home under /tmp and a HOME of their own, so they never touch your VMs or your Lima home, and they never start a VM. They run in mise run test wherever limactl is on PATH, and where it isn’t, they skip and say why.

Each test walks through scenario, which makes every kind of Lima config devvm makes, through the same code devvm runs. It makes base from Ubuntu’s image and from a --from conversion, a layer, the shared tools’ build VM, the conversion’s VM, and a project VM with its mounts, ports, size and environment. Then it makes the edits that a build’s start makes, and those of the project VM’s starts: its first start, a confined start with the proxy’s password that changes its agents’ folders, agent forwarding and size in the same edit, and an open start and one with no network. In the end it deletes everything. TestLimaConfigsValid runs limactl validate on every instance’s lima.yaml after each step. That covers the proxy’s password too, which devvm writes into lima.yaml itself, so limactl edit never checks it.

TestLimactlStubContract in contract_test.go keeps the limactl stub in internal/stubtest/stub honest, because the CLI tests and most Go tests trust it to act as Lima does. It runs scenario twice, once through the real limactl and once through the stub, and after each step it compares every instance as devvm reads it from limactl list --json. It compares the order of the instances, each one’s status, size, mounts, agent forwarding, ssh port and networks, and the edits each kind of start would make to it. When Lima and the stub differ, the test names the step and the fields that differ, and the stub gets fixed to match Lima.

Golden fixtures

The golden fixtures are what the real tools printed, kept in testdata/golden/darwin/ and testdata/golden/linux/, so the tests can check both devvm’s parsers and the stubs against real output on any machine. Each system’s folder holds what its tools printed there:

Fixture The real output of Captured from
limactl-version.txt limactl --version TestLimactlStubContract’s run on real Lima
limactl-list-stopped.json limactl list --json the contract test’s dummy instances, after the step that leaves the most
limactl-list-running.json limactl list --json of a running VM the project section’s first VM
qemu-img-info.json qemu-img info -U --output=json of base’s disk the images section, on Linux
qemu-img-info-overlay.json the same, of a project VM’s overlay disk the project section, on Linux
security-missing.txt security find-generic-password for an item that isn’t there, and its exit status the images section, on macOS
tmutil-isexcluded.txt tmutil isexcluded the images section, on macOS

mise run e2e -- --golden captures them on a real machine, into the checkout, and you commit what changed. It runs the contract test with STUB_GOLDEN set to the system’s folder for the dummy instances’ fixtures, and runs the other commands itself, so a run needs the images section, and the project section for a running VM. Each fixture has this machine’s home folder replaced with /home/me, the user’s name with me, and the user’s full name, the timezone and a VM’s environment made up, so it holds nothing of yours. A capture isn’t a check, so a run with --golden runs as many checks as one without, and a capture that fails says so and keeps the fixture it had. Run it on a Mac and on a Linux host after Lima or QEMU changes what it prints.

TestGoldenLimactlVersion, TestGoldenLimactlList and TestGoldenQemuImgInfo in internal/backend/lima/golden_test.go read every system’s fixtures with devvm’s own parsers, so a change in what the tools print that devvm would misread fails them on any machine. Each also runs the stub and checks that its output has the same form, or the same shape for JSON: every field the stub prints is one that the real tool prints, with a value of the same kind. For limactl list --json, the stub’s output is its listing after the contract test’s scenario. TestGoldenSecurityTmutil in internal/platform checks the stub’s security and tmutil against macOS’s fixtures the same way, on macOS.

Unreviewed emulations

devvm refuses an emulated feature until its review passes, yet the review needs end-to-end checks of it. In a test build, DEVVM_UNREVIEWED lets the ones it names through, as backend:feature pairs, comma-separated, each time with a warning (backend_unreviewed_used). A release ignores it:

DEVVM_UNREVIEWED=lima:ports-all devvm

It’s for tests only, of an emulation before its review: none needs it now, as every emulation is reviewed. It never makes a feature a backend lacks usable, and devvm doctor still shows the feature unreviewed.

A host of any size

devvm reads this machine’s CPUs, its memory and the free space on its disks when it fits base to the host, checks a size you give it, checks free space before a build or a new VM, and warns in devvm doctor. All of these reads go through platform.Host, so the CLI tests can stand in for a host of any size and pass the same way on a large Mac and on a small CI runner. In a test build, three environment variables replace what platform.Host reads:

Variable Replaces
DEVVM_TEST_CPUS the number of CPUs
DEVVM_TEST_MEMORY_GIB the memory, in GiB
DEVVM_TEST_FREE_GIB the free space in GiB, on every disk

Only a test build reads them, and a release ignores all three, so no variable can make devvm see more free space or more memory than this machine has. Each one that isn’t set leaves the machine’s own value. internal/cli/script_test.go sets a large host in every script: 8 CPUs, 16 GiB of memory and 500 GiB free, which is more than base asks for and more than any build checks for. A script that tests a small host sets its own values with env, as small_host.txtar does with 2 CPUs, 7 GiB and 1 GiB free:

env DEVVM_TEST_CPUS=2
env DEVVM_TEST_MEMORY_GIB=7
! exec devvm size -g --cpus 3
stderr '^devvm: too_many_cpus have=2 want=3$'

To go back to the large host later in the same script, set the large values again, because an empty value leaves the machine’s own. The fake host covers only size and free space. What differs between operating systems, such as Lima’s disk floors on Linux, ports already in use, Docker on PATH, or tmpfs and 9p mounts, still differs, and the Linux CI job is what catches it.

Any time zone

The tests pass in any time zone and on any date, because a test that compares times counts them from an instant it parsed or fixed, or works in UTC, and never sets time.Local. A testscript that needs an old file uses a date far in the past, such as touch -t 202001010000, and one that needs a file that stays new uses a date far in the future, such as an export named 20991231-235959, so the scripts keep passing as the calendar moves on. CI runs mise run test in UTC on macOS and Linux, and a third job runs it on Linux with TZ=America/Los_Angeles, which has daylight saving time, so a test that only passes in one zone fails in CI and not only on a laptop. To check a change the same way, run the tests with another zone, including one with an odd offset or a half-hour DST change:

TZ=America/Los_Angeles mise run test
TZ=Pacific/Chatham mise run test
TZ=Australia/Lord_Howe mise run test

Fuzzing

go test runs only the seed inputs of each fuzz target, so the Fuzz workflow in .github/workflows/fuzz.yml fuzzes every target for two minutes each Monday, and you can start it by hand from the Actions tab. It finds the targets by reading each func Fuzz in the tests, so a new target is fuzzed without any change to the workflow, and the proxy’s targets run first. When a target fails, the workflow uploads the input that broke it as an artifact named crash-<target>. Put that file in the package’s testdata/fuzz/<target>/ folder, fix the code, and commit both, because go test then runs the input as a seed every time. To fuzz one target on your machine, run go test -run '^$' -fuzz '^FuzzParseRule$' -fuzztime 1m ./internal/proxy.

Manual checks

What the end-to-end tests leave out, as it would change something of yours or needs something it doesn’t have:

  • Screen Sharing on devvm desktop: e2e speaks VNC itself (TestE2EDesktop), because it can’t drive a window. In a VM made with --layers desktop, run devvm desktop. Screen Sharing opens and asks for the password devvm shows, and the Xfce desktop answers the mouse and keys. A wrong password gets refused. With Edit > Use Shared Clipboard on, text you copy on this machine doesn’t paste in the VM, and with devvm desktop --clipboard it does. ~/.local/share/devvm/logs/runs/ has no line saying the relay doesn’t know a message (which the relay doesn't know).

  • A VM’s clock after this machine sleeps: e2e can’t sleep a Mac, and hosted CI can’t either. With an open VM and an allowlist VM running, compare each VM’s date +%s.%N over ssh with this machine’s clock, halfway through the ssh round trip. Then sleep the Mac for over 30 minutes and compare again right after it wakes and 2 minutes later. Each VM stays within about 0.1 s of this machine, the same as before the sleep, and the clock catches up without NTP: chrony in the allowlist VM has never synced, yet it stays right, while chrony in each VM logs Forward time jump detected! after the wake. Before you sleep the Mac, check that pmset -g assertions shows PreventSystemSleep 0. An app running caffeinate -s on AC power turns a sleep into a dark wake where the CPU keeps running, so the VMs never pause and the check proves nothing. In a real sleep, a measurement you run every few minutes in the background leaves a gap.

  • --from an image only Docker has (built locally, never pushed): it would build an image in your Docker. Build a small one (docker build -t devvm-local-test . from a Dockerfile with FROM alpine:3), run devvm --from devvm-local-test in a new folder, check the VM boots from it, then devvm rm and docker image rm devvm-local-test.

item.title: Maintaining
item.description:
For maintainers: version bumps and releases. Run the scripts with mise, which puts the pinned GoReleaser and minisign on PATH: mise exec -- scripts/release.sh.

Updating pinned versions

  • scripts/bump.sh --check lists every pin against upstream; scripts/bump.sh [tool...] rewrites the pins (all tools by default) and prints a summary for the commit message. It writes a value only if it has the shape of a pin (a version, a 64-hex checksum, a dated release, a commit), since some of the edited files run on the host, and edits nothing unless every value is good. It needs curl and jq. When upstream’s latest is older than a pin, as when a release marker hasn’t moved yet, --check says the pin is newer and bump.sh leaves it as it is.
  • Every Monday the Pins workflow (.github/workflows/pins.yml) runs scripts/bump.sh --check and opens or updates one issue, “Pinned versions to bump”, which lists the outdated pins, and closes it once none is left. It never bumps anything: you run scripts/bump.sh with the tools it lists, then the --from tier of the end-to-end tests, because pin bumps change images.
  • The tools: docker, nix, direnv, nix-direnv, mise, rustup, crane, omb, eza, tealdeer, e2e-tools, e2e-from, e2e-ubuntu, e2e-lima. base’s Ubuntu cloud image and its apt packages have nothing to bump: devvm pins the newest image on each machine at its first build of base, and records the newest packages for each key of base at its first build (Ubuntu’s cloud image, base’s packages). docker moves Docker’s packages (assets/layers/docker.sh), read from its repository for base’s Ubuntu release, and its signing key. Packages added to assets/layers/base.sh or assets/features/ need no pin of their own: they change base’s key, whose first build records them.
  • mise moves base’s mise (assets/layers/base.sh) and devvm’s host mise (internal/tools/mise.go) together: the host one writes the lock base’s installs from. TestMisePins fails when their versions or Linux checksums differ, and base’s mise version is in the key of each tool image mise installs, so a bump builds them again.
  • The shared tools aren’t pinned for users: holds go in assets/shared-tools/mise.toml (node = "24" stays on that major). testdata/mise.lock is a fixed lock for the tests.
  • Their backends are named in mise.toml’s [tool_alias] table, for every tool that isn’t one of mise’s own core: tools, because mise’s registry can move a tool to another backend in any release (versions). A new shared tool gets its alias there, and TestToolBackendsNamed fails when a tool that isn’t a core: tool has none, or when its alias isn’t the backend that tests/e2e-mise.lock resolved.
  • When opencode’s major version changes, or a bump of e2e-tools moves opencode to a version that adds migrations, refresh internal/vm/testdata/opencode-<version>.sql, the schema of opencode’s database that TestOpencodeCleanSchema cleans. Print it with sqlite3 ~/.local/share/opencode/opencode.db .schema in a VM with that opencode, after opencode auth list has made the database, and copy only the schema, never rows. Name the file for the version, and in the test put each new table in its list of tables that devvm empties or keeps, which the test asks for. A table or a column that holds a login also goes into opencodeLogins (internal/vm/agents.go) and the design note’s opencode’s database in history exports.
  • e2e-tools, e2e-from and e2e-ubuntu move the end-to-end tests’ own pins, which keep their cached images valid between runs: e2e-tools resolves tests/e2e-mise.lock again, with devvm’s pinned host mise, for both architectures’ glibc and musl VMs, and refuses a tool whose download has no checksum on every platform yet; e2e-from moves the digests of node:24, alpine:3 and ubuntu:26.04 in tests/e2e/from_test.go to Docker Hub’s; e2e-ubuntu moves e2eUbuntuRelease in tests/e2e/sandbox_test.go, the dated release of Ubuntu’s cloud image that e2e pins base to in place of the newest, to the newest Ubuntu lists. Ubuntu removes dated releases after a few months, and e2e’s going stops its first builds of base: bump e2e-ubuntu before that. Run e2e-tools after any change to assets/shared-tools/mise.toml, because the end-to-end tests refuse a lock resolved from another one (end-to-end tests). mise run test catches it first: TestE2ELockPins checks the lock’s first line against mise.toml and that it locks each of its tools, and TestE2EUbuntuPins checks that e2eUbuntuRelease is a dated release of base’s Ubuntu release, which e2e-ubuntu lists, and that scripts/bump.sh and tests/e2e name only that release.
  • e2e-lima moves the Lima release that CI’s end-to-end workflow installs, LIMA_VERSION in .github/workflows/e2e.yml, to Lima’s newest release, and LIMA_SHA256 to its Linux-x86_64 tarball’s line in that release’s SHA256SUMS. Lima’s release notes print the SHA-256 of SHA256SUMS itself, so e2e-lima checks the downloaded file against that value first and edits nothing when they differ.
  • assets/layers/ubuntu-cloud.gpg is Ubuntu’s cloud image signing key (fingerprint D2EB44626FDDC30B513D5BB71A5D6C4C7DB87C81), from keyserver.ubuntu.com. If Ubuntu changes it, pinning a new image (a first build of base, or devvm rebuild base) stops with ubuntu_bad_signature: fetch the new key, check its fingerprint against Ubuntu’s announcement, and replace the file (gpg --export FPR).
  • assets/layers/ubuntu-archive.gpg is Ubuntu’s archive signing key, “Ubuntu Archive Automatic Signing Key (2018)” (fingerprint F6ECB3762474EDA9D21B7022871920D1991BC93C), fetched from keyserver.ubuntu.com by that fingerprint, checked against the fingerprint that Ubuntu’s security team lists, and exported with gpg --export-options export-minimal --export FPR. devvm checks the InRelease files of a first build of base against it (ubuntu.ArchiveKeyring). If Ubuntu signs the archive with a new key, that build stops with packages_refused: fetch the new key, check its fingerprint the same way, and replace the file. The key must be RSA, because internal/ubuntu/pgp.go checks only RSA signatures. Moving base to a new Ubuntu release (ubuntu.Series, ubuntu.Version) also moves ubuntu.Released, the day Ubuntu released it, which is the date of that release’s own InRelease (dists/<series>/InRelease), because devvm refuses a release pocket dated before it.
  • Edited scripts change image keys, so the affected images rebuild on next use. An edit to assets/prelude.sh changes the key of every image and every shared tool image. Build them in a sandbox of their own (LIMA_HOME, DEVVM_LIMA_HOME, XDG_DATA_HOME, XDG_CONFIG_HOME) before committing (devvm build docker, or a VM made with the tools whose build script changed), then devvm gc, and run the end-to-end tests.

Checking base against Ubuntu’s newest

The end-to-end tests pin base to e2eUbuntuRelease, so they never build base the way a user’s first build does, from Ubuntu’s newest cloud image and the mirrors’ newest packages. An upstream change can break those builds before any test sees it. For example, vz’s direct kernel boot needs an uncompressed arm64 kernel, and a VM shuts down only when its kernel has gpio_keys. mise run e2e -- --newest-base builds base as a user’s first build does and runs the checks that prove it works: images, then project (a VM that boots, stops, starts again and shuts down) and tools. --only chooses other sections in their place.

The run gives devvm no release to pin. It reads the newest release from Ubuntu’s listing, as scripts/bump.sh e2e-ubuntu does, and prints it at its start next to e2eUbuntuRelease. It runs in a sandbox of its own, which is slot 0’s with -newest added to its Lima home, state folder, Keychain service and lock (~/.lt-e2e-go-newest, /tmp/devvm-go-e2e-newest, devvm-go-e2e-newest and /tmp/devvm-go-e2e-newest.lock), with each fixed port slot 0’s plus 1000. So the cached pinned images in the other sandboxes stay as they are. Each run first deletes its sandbox’s images, tool images and package cache, so base is built from nothing, with its packages from the mirrors. The images section checks that devvm pinned the release Ubuntu listed as its newest and that base booted from it. When the newest doesn’t boot, a user’s devvm falls back to the release before it (origin_no_boot), so that check fails on the fallback. Its times go in timings/plain-newest/ in slot 0’s state folder, apart from the cached runs’. --newest-base can’t be combined with --slots or --slot.

Run it before each release and every week or two between them, on an arm64 Mac (vz) and on a Linux host (QEMU) when you can, because the two boot base differently. At its end, it prints the release Ubuntu listed and the release devvm pinned. When a check fails, it says UPSTREAM DRIFT and names the release, because a user’s first build of base gets the same failure now. Then:

  1. Read the failed check’s output and the run log of base’s build, which the build’s output names (log_details), in the sandbox’s state folder under data/devvm/logs/runs/.
  2. Run mise run e2e -- --only images on the pinned release. If it passes, the failure is upstream’s, from the newer image or its packages. If it fails too, the fault is devvm’s own, so fix that first.
  3. Fix devvm for the new release, such as a change to assets/layers/base.sh or to the Lima template. Then run --newest-base again until it passes.
  4. Bump e2e-ubuntu to that release once it passes, so the other end-to-end runs test it too.

Until a fix ships, users can still build base, because devvm’s fallback to the release before covers a newest release that doesn’t boot. A package that breaks base has no fallback, so a fix for one goes in the next release.

Releasing

  • Once, the keys: a minisign key for releases, minisign -G -p packaging/minisign.pub -s ~/.minisign/devvm.key (commit packaging/minisign.pub; the secret key and its password never go in the repo), and a key git signs tags with (git config user.signingkey, GPG, or SSH with gpg.format ssh) that git tag -v verifies on this machine. Commit its fingerprint in packaging/release-signer, one per line (# comments): the GPG fingerprint (gpg --fingerprint, no spaces), or the SSH key’s SHA256:… (ssh-keygen -lf KEY.pub). release.sh refuses a tag signed by any other key, even one git trusts. To rotate, add the new key’s line, tag with it, then remove the old one.

  • Each release: bump VERSION, add the CHANGELOG.md entry and commit it on main. Then tag main’s HEAD with git tag -s v<version> and run mise exec -- scripts/publish.sh, which asks for the minisign password once and asks once more before it publishes anything. The secret key never leaves this machine, and only minisign reads it, so no CI job and no GitHub secret ever has it.

  • A prerelease, such as a release candidate or a beta, goes out the same way, with a version of the form x.y.z-<word>.N: VERSION holds 0.2.0-rc.1, CHANGELOG.md gets an entry ## 0.2.0-rc.1, and the tag is v0.2.0-rc.1. The word is lowercase letters, such as rc, beta or alpha, and release.sh refuses any other form of VERSION. scripts/publish.sh marks a prerelease’s GitHub release as a prerelease, passing --prerelease to gh release create and gh release edit, so GitHub’s latest release skips it, and so do the install script’s default, devvm upgrade and the daily release check. In the tap it changes only Formula/devvm-rc.rb, the formula that follows prereleases, in a commit titled devvm-rc <version>, so the formula devvm stays on the last release. At the end, it prints how to check the prerelease with brew upgrade devvm-rc or brew install devvmhq/tap/devvm-rc, and the prerelease’s install script line.

  • The tap’s two formulas are devvm, the newest release’s, and devvm-rc, the newest prerelease’s or release’s, whichever is newer. devvm-rc only moves forward: each publish, a release’s or a prerelease’s, points Formula/devvm-rc.rb at the version it publishes, unless the tap’s devvm-rc already names a newer one. So a release moves devvm-rc users onto it once it’s newer than their prerelease, and a patch release of an older line, or a prerelease older than the tap’s, leaves devvm-rc where it is. The printout says which way it goes, and when nothing in the tap changes, as for such a prerelease, it has no tap step and prints the install script line and devvm upgrade --to for checking it.

  • A prerelease’s changelog entry lists what changed since the version before it, whether that’s a release or another prerelease, and it becomes that prerelease’s notes on GitHub. When the release itself goes out, its entry, such as ## 0.2.0, replaces its prereleases’ entries and lists everything since the last release, so someone who upgrades from that release reads one entry. Each prerelease’s notes stay on its GitHub release.

  • Before it builds, scripts/publish.sh checks what it needs and stops with nothing done when a check fails. The tag v<version> has to pass release.sh’s own checks, so it exists, is signed, and is signed by a key in packaging/release-signer. The tag’s commit has to be main’s HEAD, and origin’s main has to be an ancestor of it, so that the push is a fast-forward. If origin already has the tag, it has to be the same tag. The working tree has to be clean, gh has to be installed and logged in (gh auth status), and minisign has to be installed. A published GitHub release for the tag is refused unless it already has every file, which is the case when an earlier run stopped after it, and unless GitHub marks it as a prerelease exactly when the version is one. The refusal names the gh release edit command that fixes the mark. The tap’s checkout, a clone of devvmhq/homebrew-tap, has to exist, be clean and be on main, for a prerelease too, and its origin has to have no commits that its main lacks. The checkout is DEVVM_TAP_DIR, or ../homebrew-tap next to this repo by default.

  • Then it builds and shows the release. It runs scripts/release.sh, which builds dist/ and signs SHA256SUMS, and where minisign asks for the password. It prints the version, the tag’s commit, each file with its size and SHA-256, the release notes, which are the CHANGELOG.md entry for the version, and the tap’s changes as a git diff of each formula it writes: Formula/devvm.rb for a release, and Formula/devvm-rc.rb, with a line saying when a release moves it too, or when it stays on a newer version. It lists the four steps, each marked done or to do, and when nothing in the tap changes, the fourth says so. Then it asks Publish devvm <version>? [y/N] on the terminal, and any answer but y stops it with nothing published. --dry-run stops before the question, so it pushes and publishes nothing and makes no commit in the tap, and --help describes the script.

  • Then it publishes, in this order. It pushes main and then the tag to origin. It makes the GitHub release devvmhq/devvm v<version> with gh release create --verify-tag, titled devvm <version>, with the release notes and the archives, the source tarball, SHA256SUMS, SHA256SUMS.minisig and install.sh. The release starts as a draft and is published only once every file is uploaded, so nobody sees a release that is missing files. Last, it copies dist/devvm.rb to the tap’s Formula/devvm.rb and dist/devvm-rc.rb to its Formula/devvm-rc.rb, each only when it’s one the tap gets and it differs, commits them in one commit, devvm <version> for a release or devvm-rc <version> for a prerelease, with the tap’s own commit signing, and pushes the tap. It uses gh for GitHub and never puts a GitHub token on a command line. At the end it prints how to check the release: brew update && brew upgrade devvm, or brew trust --formula devvmhq/tap/devvm and then brew install devvmhq/tap/devvm, with devvm-rc in place of devvm for a prerelease, and the install script’s curl line.

  • When a step fails, it says which steps it published and which it didn’t. Fix what failed and run it again, because every step skips what’s already done: a pushed main or tag, a published release whose SHA256SUMS matches the new build’s, and a tap whose formulas are already this build’s. A draft release that an earlier run left gets this build’s files again before it’s published. A release published from another build, whose SHA256SUMS doesn’t match, is refused. To finish by hand instead, run the steps it didn’t do in order: git push origin main, git push origin v<version>, the gh release create above (or gh release upload --clobber to a draft, then gh release edit v<version> --draft=false), each with --prerelease for a prerelease, and then copy the formulas the printout listed, dist/devvm.rb and dist/devvm-rc.rb, to the tap’s Formula/, commit them and push it.

  • scripts/release.sh checks the tag with git tag -v and its signer against this checkout’s packaging/release-signer, then builds dist/ from the tagged commit with GoReleaser (.goreleaser.yaml), in a clone of its own, so only what’s committed goes in, with one goreleaser release --skip=publish. It checks that the binary built for this host prints the version, writes install.sh and adds its checksum to SHA256SUMS, then signs SHA256SUMS with ~/.minisign/devvm.key (or DEVVM_MINISIGN_KEY) and verifies it with packaging/minisign.pub. Nothing is published, because publishing is scripts/publish.sh’s. scripts/release.sh --check runs only the tag’s checks and the build’s preconditions, prints the tag’s commit and builds nothing, and scripts/publish.sh runs it first.

  • dist/ then holds:

    File What
    devvm-<version>-<os>-<arch>.tar.gz the binary, its files (assets/) embedded, with README.md, CHANGELOG.md and LICENSE, for darwin and linux, arm64 and amd64
    devvm-<version>.tar.gz the source, attached to the release for whoever wants to build devvm themselves
    SHA256SUMS, SHA256SUMS.minisig their checksums and install.sh’s, and the signature
    install.sh the install script, set to this release and to packaging/minisign.pub’s key
    devvm-rc.rb the Homebrew formula devvm-rc, which follows prereleases, set to each platform’s archive, its URL and its checksum from SHA256SUMS
    devvm.rb for a release, not a prerelease, the Homebrew formula devvm, set the same way

  • scripts/release.sh --head builds from HEAD’s commit instead, for testing, with VERSION’s version, a release’s or a prerelease’s. It’s unsigned unless DEVVM_MINISIGN_KEY names a test key; DEVVM_MINISIGN_PUB names its public key in place of packaging/minisign.pub. DEVVM_RELEASE_URL points the formula at a test location. A commit without install.sh is refused.

  • scripts/release.sh --formula-from DIR writes only the formulas, for VERSION’s release once it’s published, and builds nothing: dist/devvm-rc.rb, and dist/devvm.rb too when VERSION isn’t a prerelease. Download the release’s SHA256SUMS and SHA256SUMS.minisig into DIR first. The script checks the signature against packaging/minisign.pub, and that its trusted comment is devvm <version> for VERSION’s version, so it refuses another release’s files. Then it fills in the formulas the same way a build does, from that SHA256SUMS.

  • To try dist/install.sh on such a build, copy dist/ to DIR/releases/download/v<version>/, then in a throwaway HOME with DEVVM_PREFIX under it: DEVVM_INSTALL_TEST=1 source dist/install.sh, set repo_url=file://DIR and protos='=https,file' (it downloads over HTTPS only), and run main --no-deps. Without --no-deps it offers to install what the host lacks: answer no, or run it with no terminal.

  • Every build sets the version with -X github.com/devvmhq/devvm/internal/cli.version=<version>: devvm doesn’t read VERSION. The formula template (packaging/homebrew/devvm.rb) is both formulas’ one source, and it builds nothing. It has an archive for each of macOS and Linux on arm64 and Intel, the same archives the install script installs, and it installs the binary alone from the one for this machine. release.sh fills in each formula’s class, Devvm or DevvmRc, and the other formula, which it conflicts with by its full name, devvmhq/tap/devvm-rc or devvmhq/tap/devvm, because both install the devvm command. It also fills in each archive’s URL and its checksum, which it reads from the SHA256SUMS it just wrote, on every line that isn’t a comment. Both generated formulas pass brew audit --strict --online and brew style.

  • Publishing is the maintainer’s call, so an agent asks first and never runs scripts/publish.sh without --dry-run on its own. The script’s tests (testdata/script/publish.txtar) run it against a local bare repo as origin, a local bare tap and a fake gh.

The docs sites

The docs have two sites, and the Docs workflow (.github/workflows/docs.yml) deploys both. devvm.dev shows the docs of the latest release, so what users read matches the devvm they install. next.devvm.dev shows the docs on main, for the next release, which is what someone trying a prerelease reads. A pull request that touches the docs gets their lints and a build, and it deploys nothing, so a pull request from a fork never reaches either site or its keys.

  • devvm.dev is GitHub Pages, in the repo’s github-pages environment, which accepts deployments from main and from v* tags, and only admins can create a v* tag. When a release is published, and it isn’t a prerelease, the workflow builds the docs in that release’s tag and deploys them. A release event runs the workflow file that the tag has, so a release whose tag predates this workflow doesn’t deploy on its own. Pushes to main never change devvm.dev.
  • To deploy a release’s docs by hand, for a release that didn’t deploy on its own or to put devvm.dev back on a release, run the Docs workflow from main in the repo’s Actions tab, or with gh workflow run docs.yml --repo devvmhq/devvm -f site=devvm.dev -f ref=v0.1.0. The site is devvm.dev unless you choose another one, and the ref is the release’s tag, which has to look like v0.1.0, so a prerelease’s tag is refused. Without a ref, the workflow deploys the latest release, as gh release view names it.
  • next.devvm.dev is Cloudflare Pages, serving the files on the main branch of the repo devvmhq/docs-next, and Cloudflare builds nothing. On each push to main that touches the docs, the workflow lints and builds main’s docs for next.devvm.dev, then replaces everything in devvmhq/docs-next but its README.md with the build, and commits it as Build from devvm <short sha>. When the build is the same as the last one, it commits nothing. gh workflow run docs.yml --repo devvmhq/devvm -f site=next.devvm.dev runs it by hand. Nobody edits devvmhq/docs-next by hand, because the next build replaces it.
  • The deploy key that pushes to devvmhq/docs-next is the secret DOCS_NEXT_DEPLOY_KEY in the docs-next environment, which only main can deploy from. It’s an ed25519 key with write access to devvmhq/docs-next and to nothing else. The workflow checks that repo out with it only after the site is built, so the build never sees the key. To rotate it, make a new key, add its public half to devvmhq/docs-next as a deploy key with write access, put its private half in the secret, then delete the old deploy key.
  • The next build is hugo -s docs --minify --config hugo.yaml,next.yaml, which reads docs/next.yaml over docs/hugo.yaml. It sets the site’s address to https://next.devvm.dev/ and puts a banner on every page that says these docs are for the next devvm and links to devvm.dev. It also sets noindex, so Hextra gives every page a noindex, nofollow robots meta tag, and docs/layouts/robots.txt disallows everything, so search engines don’t index the site. devvm.dev’s build, hugo -s docs --minify, never reads docs/next.yaml, so it has no banner, its pages say index, follow, and its robots.txt allows everything.

item.title: The structure test and owners
item.description:
The structure test

internal/structure parses every Go file in the repo, tests and every platform’s included, generated files left out, and checks what linters don’t. mise run test runs it. Each failure starts with its rule and the file and line:

Rule Checks
max-methods no type has more than 24 methods, value and pointer receivers together, and no interface declares more than 24, not counting the interfaces it embeds; a larger one splits by what its methods do
no-init no func init()
package-vars a package-level var is a blank interface check, an Err*/err* sentinel from errors.New or fmt.Errorf, a regexp.MustCompile, template.Must or sync.Once* result, a //go:embed file, or listed in allowedVars; anything else becomes a field, a const or a local
layers which packages import which, in non-test files (tests may wire packages together)
owners in non-test files, only its owner runs a host command that commands lists, only the files execSites lists make a host command, only guardOwner asserts a backend package’s type, only envOwner reads a DEVVM_ variable, but the settings envSettings lists, only its file in envOwners reads HOME, only its owner’s string literals hold a text that literals lists, only its owner’s string literals are, whole, a name that names lists, only its owner’s calls to package strings split or join on a separator that separators lists, only pathsOwner builds a path in devvm’s data or config folder, and only its file in callers calls a function that callers lists (details)

The layers:

  • Only cmd/devvm and internal/cli import internal/ui; only internal/cli imports internal/vm; only cmd/devvm imports internal/cli.
  • internal/backend/... imports none of internal/vm, build, tools, netpolicy, secrets, project, gitprotect, sshconfig, sshagent, trust or vmssh, so the port forwarder and the link sessions stay devvm’s on every backend.
  • Only internal/backend/registry and internal/cli import a backend (lima); only tests import backendtest and internal/stubtest and the packages below it, which import only internal/msg and each other. The stubs’ binary, internal/stubtest/stub, and its state, internal/stubtest/stubstate, import nothing else of devvm’s, because the binary stands in for the tools devvm runs and is built apart from it.
  • internal/proxy imports no other devvm package but internal/daemon and internal/safefile.
  • assets, locales, internal/platform, internal/msg/gen, internal/testbuild, internal/hostgit, internal/shell, internal/vmname, internal/daemon, internal/fetch, internal/jsonc, internal/redact, internal/agents and internal/safefile import no devvm package; internal/agentlogin only internal/agents, internal/fetch, internal/jsonc, internal/proxy, internal/safefile and internal/state, because it holds agents’ logins; internal/msg only locales; internal/paths only internal/msg; internal/state only internal/msg, internal/paths, internal/platform and internal/vmname; internal/image only assets, internal/agents, internal/msg and internal/paths; internal/devcontainer only internal/image, internal/jsonc, internal/msg and internal/shell.

Everything it holds the code to is in devvm() in internal/structure/structure_test.go:

  • largeTypes lists the types allowed more methods, which are paths.Dirs and ui.UI, each with its count as its maximum and why. A backend isn’t one of them, because its methods are split by backend.Backend’s roles (how a backend plugs in). One that grows fails; one that shrinks fails until its maximum is lowered.
  • allowedVars lists the other package-level vars, by package folder and name, each with why: values set by -ldflags, fixed tables, test fixtures. An entry whose var is gone fails.
  • layers is the layering table: a layer’s packages (from, but not exceptFrom) import none of to (but exceptTo); x/... is x and the packages below it.
  • commands maps a host command to the one package that runs it. execSites lists the files that make a host command with exec.Command or exec.CommandContext, each with why, and a listed file that no longer makes one fails. guardOwner names internal/backend/guard.go, the one file that asserts a backend’s type. envOwner names the one file that reads devvm’s DEVVM_ variables. envSettings lists the variables read elsewhere, each with the files that read it and why. A listed file that no longer reads its variable fails. envOwners maps another variable to the one file that reads it, which for HOME is internal/paths/dirs.go.
  • literals maps a text that only one package’s string literals may hold to that package and what the others use instead. names maps a name that only one package’s string literals may be, whole, to that package and what the others use, and namesFree lists the folders whose literals may be one anyway: internal/stubtest, whose stubs are named after the commands they stand in for.
  • callers maps a function to the one file outside its package that calls it, and a listed file that no longer calls it fails. A method is listed as pkg.Type.Name, such as internal/paths.Dirs.AgentSettings, and any call of a method by that name outside its package counts, because the check reads no types, so a listed method’s name is its type’s alone.

TestRulesFail breaks each rule, and each layer, on small sources and checks the failure names it.

One owner for each concern

Each concern in devvm has one owner, the package or function that does it, such as internal/hostgit for every git command devvm runs on the host, internal/paths for every folder and file devvm uses, internal/settings for every default (settings.Read and settings.Save, over config.toml and settings.json, with each value’s parser), and locales/en.toml for every message. Before you add a helper, a parser, a path, a file reader, a message or a table, find its owner and extend it. A second copy drifts from the first, and then one of them is wrong. AGENTS.md’s layout table names the owners, and so do the failures of the checks below.

The checks on owners

An owner gets a check only when a second copy would be a bug or a security hole, and only when the check is exact, so that it never fails on code that’s right. Each check’s failure names the owner. The table is written from ownerDocs in internal/structure/owners_doc_test.go, which TestOwnersDoc checks it against and TestOwnersAgree checks against the structure test’s own tables, so a change to a check changes its row there, and go test ./internal/structure -run TestOwnersDoc -update writes the table again:

Check Owner Allowed elsewhere
forbidigo, testbuild.On internal/cli, whose readOverrides is the only code that asks whether this is a test build nowhere: other packages take the overrides as fields
forbidigo, os.FindProcess, syscall.Kill, unix.Kill and os.Process’s Kill and Signal internal/daemon, which signals a background process only while its pid file and its arguments say it’s still that process (Proc), or through the process it started (Handle) internal/platform; tests, which signal the children they started; and a child that hasn’t been waited for yet, whose pid is still its own, with a nolint saying so
forbidigo, unicode.IsGraphic, IsPrint, IsControl and Bidi_Control msg.Safe in internal/msg/safe.go, the one rule for which characters reach the terminal, which msg.Printable, msg.OneLine, the UI’s renderers and devvm agent save’s diff follow, so a second rule can’t let through what this one refuses (Colors says what it refuses) a check that isn’t about the terminal, such as a path one line long, with a //nolint:forbidigo saying so
forbidigo, HTTP clients internal/fetch, whose NewClient sets each client’s timeout and redirect policy (HTTPSOnly or SameScheme), and whose Retry, Transient, ReadCapped, Get, Resolve and Download try again after the failures that may pass, cap what a body or a download may hold, follow a HEAD’s redirects to where they end and check a download’s SHA-256 before anything uses it. fetch.Client is its own type, so a client that NewClient didn’t make, such as &fetch.Client{}, fails every request, and a caller changes a client’s transport through its Transport method internal/proxy, which is the standard library only, and tests, which make their own servers’ clients
forbidigo, os.WriteFile, os.Create and os.O_TRUNC internal/state, whose WriteFile and WriteFileMode write a file whole through a temporary file in its folder, renamed over it, so a reader never sees half of it internal/proxy, which imports only the standard library and has its own writer, writeAtomic; internal/msg/gen, which imports no devvm package; internal/stubtest; tests; and, with a nolint saying why, a file written another way: a log that a process writes as it runs, a download that streams into its file, and internal/daemon’s pid and status files, each written in one write that a reader takes as missing until its line ends
forbidigo, os.Open, os.OpenFile, os.ReadFile, os.OpenRoot, os.OpenInRoot, os.DirFS and os.Root’s Open, OpenFile, ReadFile and FS, in the code that reads files a VM can write or swap: internal/gitprotect, internal/agentlogin, internal/vm’s devcontainer.go, detect.go and agentsave*.go, internal/netpolicy/rules.go, and internal/proxy’s config.go and policy.go internal/safefile, which imports only the standard library, so the proxy reads with it too. Its Read and Open open a file without blocking and, unless the caller passes Follow, without following a symbolic link at the path’s end. They then check the file they opened, not its name, so a FIFO, a device or a folder is refused with ErrNotRegular, a file past its cap with ErrTooLong, and, with OneLink, a file with another hard link with ErrLinked. A FIFO that the VM swaps in after a check can’t hold devvm, and a link to /dev/zero can’t flood it. OpenRoot opens beneath a folder through os.Root, never through a link out of it, and its FS lists and stats what’s there but opens only regular files every other file, which is devvm’s own or the user’s; tests, which make their own fixtures; and, with a nolint saying why, what opens a file to write it or a folder to lock it
forbidigo, os.Setenv, os.Unsetenv, os.Clearenv and syscall’s each command’s own environment, its exec.Cmd’s Env, because every command and background process devvm starts inherits devvm’s. A VM’s SSH agent is one: the finder’s target carries its socket, which goes to the backend in backend.ExecOpts.Agent, backend.ShellOpts.Agent and Confinement.AgentSocket, and Lima sets SSH_AUTH_SOCK on that VM’s limactl commands alone, so a run that reaches several VMs never gives one another’s daemon.Ready in internal/daemon/status.go, which takes the status file’s name out of a background process’s own environment, and tests, which use t.Setenv
the structure test’s owners, host commands the runners: the UI’s LoggedCmd, which a package takes as a field and which runs a command into the run log, a backend’s Runner, and internal/hostgit. A host command that one of them doesn’t run is made only in the files execSites lists: those that make the command a runner then runs, such as Lima’s limactl and mise’s, and those whose command can’t go into the run log, because it streams for as long as a link, the port forwarder or the desktop’s relay lasts, asks on the terminal, outlives the run, or carries a secret tests
the structure test’s owners, a backend’s other interfaces backend.As in internal/backend/guard.go, because the registry’s backends are behind its guard, whose type has only backend.Backend’s methods, so a type assertion to backend.Forgetter or *lima.Lima on one is always false tests
the structure test’s owners, git internal/hostgit, which runs git without the repo’s fsmonitor, hooks or filters, over ssh only, without the environment’s GIT_* variables and prompts tests, which run git to make their repos
forbidigo, os.UserHomeDir, and the structure test’s owners, HOME paths.FromEnv in internal/paths/dirs.go, which reads HOME once into paths.Dirs.Home, so a test or an e2e run that sets its own HOME moves every path devvm takes from it tests
the structure test’s owners, DEVVM_ variables readOverrides in internal/cli/overrides.go, which reads a test build’s stand-ins, while a release reads none the settings in envSettings, and tests
the structure test’s owners, shell quoting internal/shell, whose Quote and QuoteJoin quote words for a POSIX shell, so a value never runs as a command tests
the structure test’s owners, the VM-name grammar internal/vmname, whose IsVM tells a project VM’s name from an image’s, so gc never takes a project VM for an image tests
the structure test’s owners, the coding agents internal/agents, whose Defs hold every fact devvm keeps of each agent, so no copy of an agent’s list or paths goes stale when one is added. A string literal that is an agent’s name or a login file’s kind, whole, or that holds an agent’s folder below the home folder, fails, and code of one agent’s own names the agent by its constant there (adding a coding agent) internal/stubtest, whose stubs are named after the commands they stand in for, and tests
the structure test’s owners, the toolchains internal/image, whose SharedTools holds every fact devvm keeps of each toolchain: its members, the files that call for it, its installer, its guest environment, its PATH folders and its version files. A string literal that is a toolchain’s name or a member’s, whole, fails, so code elsewhere asks the table, and a new toolchain is an entry there (adding a toolchain) internal/stubtest, and tests
the structure test’s owners, image names internal/image, whose Name is an image’s name and splits it into its layers (Layers, Parent, Has), whose NameOf joins layers into one, and whose ParseName reads the name the user gives, which build.Names’ Parse checks against the layers there are. devvm build, devvm rebuild and devvm images rm read their names there once, and the rest of devvm passes the image.Name on tests
the structure test’s owners, state.ReadHash and project.Parents the finder in internal/vm/finder.go, whose target finds the VM every command acts on: the folder’s own, the nearest parent folder’s under --here and --parent (resolveFolder), or one named (devvm rm VM). It finds a folder’s VM by the state that records the folder (finder.state, by the path’s hash first, then recorded), offers to move a VM whose folder moved there (moveHere in internal/vm/move.go, the match here.movedFrom), and names a new VM by the first of the folder’s names whose VM folder is free (newName, project.Nth). Its need says what the command needs of the VM, and need.check is the one place that refuses one that isn’t there, one made for an earlier folder at its path, one whose remake didn’t finish and one whose creation didn’t, the last with refuseUnfinished, which every start (starter.bringUp in internal/vm/start.go) makes too. It reads the folder devvm runs in only then, so the commands that act on no folder’s VM run in a folder that’s gone. The VM it finds is a target (internal/vm/target.go). It holds what the VM’s backend told the finder, which each start and stop of the VM then updates, and it runs what a command does with that VM: exec, shell, stop, running, ownSSH and the name of its ssh config entry internal/state, and tests
the structure test’s owners, state.ReadAll the inventory in internal/vm/inventory.go, which reads every VM’s state (ReadStates), and with ReadInventory the backends’ lists too, each within its wait, for every listing of VMs: devvm ls, devvm space, devvm images and devvm gc, the ssh config, devvm gc --orphans, the links, devvm secret’s list, finding a VM by its name and the mounts that devvm’s SSH agent checks a key against. Its one failure policy is that a backend that can’t list fails a listing (Inventory.Err) only when some VM’s state names it, and that a state that can’t be read is a row of its own, which the readers leave out and ToolsInUse and Mounts fail on. state.VMNames, which fails on such a state, stays for the readers below internal/vm: netpolicy, ports and sshconfig.ChooseAlias internal/state, and tests
the structure test’s owners, paths.Dirs.AgentSettings and paths.Dirs.AgentLogins devvm’s agent store: agentStore in internal/vm/agents.go for the agents’ settings, which the mounts, the setup’s copies, a remake’s home and devvm agent import take, and secrets.LoginFile in internal/secrets/secrets.go for their logins, which the setup’s copies and the proxy read, so nothing reads an agent’s files from the home folder but vm.AgentImport internal/paths, and tests
the structure test’s owners, paths in devvm’s folders internal/paths, whose Dirs and VM name every file and folder devvm keeps, so the layout, its golden listing in testdata/script/layout.txtar and a VM’s teardown miss none. A filepath.Join onto a Data or Config field fails, and so does an os.MkdirTemp or os.CreateTemp there whose name is a literal; a name from paths, such as paths.ToolsBuildPrefix, passes tests

forbidigo matches only the function a call names, so the checks that look at a call’s arguments are in the structure test. It finds a host command in an exec.Command or exec.CommandContext call that names it, as a literal or as a constant, whatever name the file imports os/exec under. It finds a DEVVM_ variable in a call to any function or field named Getenv or LookupEnv, in any case, so t.Getenv and a getenv parameter count as well as os.Getenv, and it finds HOME the same way. The settings envSettings lists are the ones users set, DEVVM_NO_TOOL_CHECK, DEVVM_NO_RELEASE_CHECK, DEVVM_LIMA_HOME, DEVVM_SECRET_SERVICE and DEVVM_FROM; names mode, DEVVM_MESSAGES, which any build has; and the variables devvm sets for its own processes, DEVVM_GUESTFWD for devvm _qemu and DEVVM_DAEMON_STATUS for each background process internal/daemon starts.

The structure test also finds a copy of an owner’s code by its text, in literals. A string literal outside tests that holds '\'', the escaped quote a shell quoter writes, belongs in internal/shell, and one that holds [0-9a-f]{14}, the hash at the end of a project VM’s name, belongs in internal/vmname. A quote written as a rune, such as '\'' in Go, isn’t a string literal, so it doesn’t count. One that holds a coding agent’s folder below the home folder, such as .codex/ or .pi/agent, belongs in internal/agents, and so does one that is an agent’s name or a login file’s kind, whole, such as "opencode" (names), so code of one agent’s own names it by its constant there, such as agents.Opencode, and a longer text that mentions an agent, such as a command’s example, doesn’t count. A literal that is a toolchain’s name or one of its members’, whole, such as "dotnet" or "pnpm", belongs in internal/image in the same way, so code elsewhere finds a toolchain’s facts in its image.SharedTools entry. In the same way, separators finds a copy of a parser by what it splits on: a call to any function of package strings with + as an argument, as a literal or as a constant, splits or joins an image’s layers, so it belongs in internal/image. A call with another argument that holds a +, such as strings.ContainsAny(arg, "+,"), doesn’t count.

The shared tools have one owner too, the table image.SharedTools in internal/image/tool.go, whose agents’ entries it makes from the coding agents’ registry, agents.Defs (adding a coding agent). Each entry, an image.ToolDef, holds a tool’s name, its kind (a toolchain or an agent), its members (the tools in the lock that its name stands for, such as pnpm and bun for node), the files in a project folder that call for it, and its installer, which is mise for every tool but rust, which rustup installs, and dotnet, which assets/shared-tools/build.sh unpacks from Microsoft’s SDK archive.
